name: Cuélebre, Adult
body:
Adult Cuélebre
CR 15

XP 51,200
CE Huge dragon
Init +4; Senses dragon senses; Perception +26; Aura frightful presence (180 ft., DC 23)

DEFENSE

AC 29, touch 8, flat-footed 29 (+21 natural, –2 size)
hp 261 (18d12+144)
Fort +19, Ref +13, Will +18
DR 5/magic; Immune paralysis, sleep; SR 26

OFFENSE

Speed 50 ft., fly 200 ft. (poor)
Melee bite +28 (2d8+16/19–20), tail slap +27 (2d6+16 plus grab), 2 wings +25 (2d6+5)
Space 15 ft.; Reach 10 ft. (15 ft. with bite and tail slap)
Special Attacks breath weapon (50-ft. cone, 12d6 acid, DC 27), crush (DC 27, 2d8+15), earthquake stomp (30-ft. radius, 6d6 bludgeoning damage, DC 27), constrict (1d8+12, tail slap)

STATISTICS

Str 33, Dex 10, Con 27, Int 16, Wis 20, Cha 19
Base Atk +18; CMB +31 (+35 grapple); CMD 41 (can’t be tripped)
Feats Improved Critical (bite), Improved Initiative, Improved Vital Strike, Iron Will, Lightning Reflexes, Multiattack, Power Attack, Vital Strike, Weapon Focus (bite)
Skills Climb +32, Fly +13, Intimidate +25, Knowledge (local) +24, Perception +26, Sense Motive +26, Stealth +13, Survival +26, Swim +32
Languages Common, Draconic, Terra

ABOUT

Cuélebres favor mountains, and forests, usually making their lairs near lakes or rivers.

They are typically solitary creatures, rarely interacting with others of its kind.

Cuélebres grow larger as they age, with their scales grow thicker over the centuries, making them nearly invulnerable to attack with ordinary weapons. Eventually they stop growing, at which point they retreat to a place they call Mar Cujada, a near-mythical place unreachable by normal folk, which is full of precious stones, coins, and other treasures. No treasure hunter has ever found this place, and some wonder whether it is entirely fictional and whether ancient cuélebres facing death simply destroy their treasures and plunge their bodies into the deep in a final act of selfish avarice, so that no one else ever enjoys their plunder.

Cuélebres possess a nigh-insatiable hunger, driving them to devour livestock and villagers alike. In some stories, the local people offer it bread called boroña to appease it, though sometimes this is not enough and it must be offered first-born sons or virgins. In stories where the cuélebre is especially nasty, the villagers leave a red-hot stone in place of the bread, slaying the dragon with this ruse, though in some tales the dragon is able to save its life by flying to the nearest bay and diving into the water, cooling itself before it burned up from the inside, later returning to wreak its vengeance.
